questions.stem: Which of the following best defines globalisation?
options: The increasing integration of national economies through trade, investment, migration and information flows
The growth of international trade in goods only
The spread of one country's culture across the world
The creation of trading blocs between neighbouring countries
questions.why: Globalisation covers investment, migration and information as well as trade, which is why a trade-only definition loses marks.
whyNot: Trade is only one dimension.
Cultural spread is a consequence, not the definition.
Trading blocs are one regional form of integration.

questions.stem: What are the three roles of the World Trade Organization?
options: Administering trade rules, providing a forum for negotiation, and settling disputes
Setting the tariff rates that all members must apply
Lending money to countries with trade deficits
Fixing exchange rates between member currencies
questions.why: Members set their own tariffs within the agreed rules; the WTO administers those rules rather than setting the rates.
whyNot: Members set their own tariffs.
Lending is the role of the International Monetary Fund and World Bank.
Exchange rates are not within the WTO's remit.

questions.stem: Which of the following best defines containerisation?
options: The use of standard-sized containers to move goods, which cut the cost and time of shipping
Packaging goods in smaller units for sale in lower-income markets
Storing inventory in a central warehouse
Producing goods in sealed factories to protect quality
questions.why: Standardised handling turned loading a ship into a matter of hours rather than days.
whyNot: That is pack-size adaptation in marketing.
That is centralised warehousing.
That is unrelated to shipping.

questions.stem: Which of the following best defines structural change?
options: A long-term shift in the relative importance of the primary, secondary and tertiary sectors
A change in a company's organisational hierarchy
A change in the rate of corporation tax
A change in a country's exchange rate regime
questions.why: Manufacturing fell as a share of developed economies while services grew, and the losses were concentrated in particular industries and regions.
whyNot: That is organisational restructuring, a different topic.
That is a fiscal change.
That is a monetary arrangement.

questions.stem: Why is it argued that falling communication costs mattered more than falling tariffs?
options: Cheap communication made global supply chains possible, not just global selling
Communication costs fell further in percentage terms
Tariffs have never fallen significantly
Communication is not affected by government policy
questions.why: Without cheap coordination a business could export but could not manage production it did not stand next to.
whyNot: The size of the fall is not the argument; the capability created is.
Average tariffs have fallen substantially over decades.
Policy does affect telecommunications, but that is not the point.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an opportunity globalisation creates for a business?
options: Extending a product's life cycle by selling a mature product into a growing market
Freedom from all exchange rate exposure
Protection from low-cost foreign competitors
Shorter and simpler supply chains
questions.why: The development cost is already sunk, so the same product generates growth again in a market where it is still at the growth stage.
whyNot: Operating internationally increases currency exposure.
Globalisation removes such protection.
Supply chains typically become longer and more complex.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a threat globalisation creates for a business?
options: Reputational exposure, because conditions anywhere in the supply chain can become news everywhere
A reduction in the size of its accessible market
The impossibility of raising finance internationally
A guaranteed fall in economies of scale
questions.why: This is why international business ethics matters commercially and not only morally.
whyNot: Globalisation enlarges the accessible market.
International capital markets become more accessible.
Higher volume generally improves scale economies.

questions.stem: What effect did the growth of the global labour force have?
options: It held down wages for lower-skilled work in developed economies and raised them where the work moved
It raised wages everywhere equally
It had no measurable effect on wages
It reduced the total amount of work available worldwide
questions.why: The opening of large economies roughly doubled the labour available to internationally mobile capital.
whyNot: The effects ran in opposite directions in different places.
The wage effects are among the most studied consequences of globalisation.
Total employment rose rather than fell.

questions.stem: Why is globalisation described as a trend rather than a law?
options: Tariffs have been reimposed, investment screened and supply chains deliberately shortened
It has never actually increased
It applies only to developed economies
It is prohibited by the WTO
questions.why: Policy risk is real, so a business built entirely on current tariff levels and open supply chains carries that risk.
whyNot: Integration increased substantially over decades.
It affects all economies.
The WTO exists to facilitate trade, not prohibit integration.

questions.stem: Why does the political pressure for protectionism arise even when trade raises total output?
options: The gains are spread thinly while the losses are concentrated in particular industries and regions
Trade always reduces total output
Consumers never benefit from trade
Governments are legally required to protect industry
questions.why: Concentrated losses are politically visible and organised; diffuse gains are not, which is the origin of the pressure.
whyNot: Trade raises total output, which is the premise of the question.
Consumers benefit through lower prices and wider choice.
No such legal requirement exists.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a limitation of the WTO?
options: Multilateral negotiation has largely stalled, so liberalisation now happens mainly through regional deals
It has no members among developed economies
It cannot settle disputes at all
It sets no rules, so trade is entirely unregulated
questions.why: Enforcement also depends on the willingness of large members to comply, and critics argue the rules have favoured developed economies.
whyNot: Developed economies are among its most active members.
Dispute settlement is one of its three core roles.
It administers an extensive body of agreed rules.

questions.stem: How has globalisation affected jobs once thought safe from international competition?
options: Services such as software, accounting and design can now be delivered remotely from anywhere
Only manufacturing jobs have ever been affected
Service jobs cannot be performed across borders
Remote delivery has made services more expensive
questions.why: Cheap reliable communication made this possible, which is a sharper version of structural change than the manufacturing story.
whyNot: Services are now heavily traded.
Many services are routinely delivered internationally.
Remote delivery generally lowered the cost.

questions.stem: Why is the judgement on globalisation usually conditional on the type of business?
options: It benefits firms that can reach new markets or source more cheaply, and threatens firms whose advantage was protection
It affects all businesses identically
It benefits only multinational corporations
It threatens only businesses that export
questions.why: Saying which type the business in the source is, and why, is the answer the question is looking for.
whyNot: The effects vary enormously between businesses.
Small firms selling online have also benefited substantially.
Firms that only sell domestically face new competitors too.

questions.stem: Which of the following best defines migration in this context?
options: The movement of people between or within countries, usually in search of work
The relocation of a business's production to another country
The movement of capital between financial markets
The transfer of technology from one firm to another
questions.why: Migration fills skill gaps, affects wage growth in receiving countries and generates remittances for sending ones.
whyNot: That is off-shoring.
That is a capital flow.
That is technology transfer.

questions.stem: Which political change contributed most directly to globalisation?
options: Economies that were closed opening to trade and investment
The introduction of income tax in developed economies
The growth of local government spending
The standardisation of national holidays
questions.why: Central planning was abandoned in many countries, import substitution gave way to export-led strategies and capital controls were relaxed.
whyNot: Domestic taxation is not a driver of globalisation.
Local spending is unrelated.
That has no bearing on international integration.

questions.stem: What is meant by saying a substantial share of world trade is between parts of the same company?
options: Multinationals move components and services between their own subsidiaries across borders
Companies trade only with their direct competitors
All trade is conducted through government agencies
Trade statistics exclude multinational activity
questions.why: This is what the increased significance of MNCs means in practice, and it is also why transfer pricing matters.
whyNot: Intra-firm trade is trade within one group, not between competitors.
Most trade is conducted by private businesses.
Multinational activity is a large part of recorded trade.
